prompt: Let $a_0,a_1,\ldots a_n$ be such that $a_n\ne0$ and $$(1+x+x^3)^{341}(1+2x+x^2+2x^3+2x^4+x^6)^{342}=\sum_{i=0}^{n}a_ix^i.$$ Find the number of odd numbers in the sequence $a_0,a_1,\ldots a_n$.
reviewNote: Official key says 3, treating the product as $(1+x+x^3)^{2^{10}}$ mod 2. But $341+2\cdot342=1025$, so the product is $(1+x+x^3)^{1025}$ mod 2, which has 9 odd coefficients (checked by computer).

prompt: Let $F_0=1$, $F_1=1$ and $F_k=F_{k-1}+F_{k-2}$. Let $P(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{99}x^{F_k}$. The remainder when $P(x)$ is divided by $x^3-1$ can be expressed as $ax^2+bx+c$. Find $2a+b$.

Let $a_n$ be the number of permutations of the numbers $S=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ such that for all $k$ with $1\le k\le n$, the sum of $k$ and the number in the $k$th position of the permutation is a power of 2. Compute $a_{2^0}+a_{2^1}+\cdots+a_{2^{20}}$.

Three identical balls are painted white and black, so that half of each sphere is a white hemisphere, and the other half is a black one. The three balls are placed on a plane surface, each with a random orientation, so that each ball has a point of contact with the other two. What is the probability that at at least one point of contact between two of the balls, both balls are the same color?
Compute the greatest positive integer $n$ such that there exists an odd integer $a$, for which $\dfrac{a^{2^n}-1}{4^{4^4}}$ is not an integer.

You are blind and cannot feel the difference between a coin that is heads up or tails up. There are 100 coins in front of you and are told that exactly 10 of them are heads up. Explain how you can split the otherwise indistinguishable coins into two groups so that both groups have the same number of heads.
answer: Split off any 10 coins into one group; flip all 10 coins in that group. Both groups then have the same number of heads.

solutions.title: Flip a group of 10
solutions.body:
Separate any 10 coins into one group, leaving 90 in the other, and flip over every coin in the group of 10.

Suppose $k$ of the 10 chosen coins were heads (you do not know $k$). The group of 90 then has $10-k$ heads. After flipping, the group of 10 has $10-k$ heads too. So both groups have the same number of heads.

**Answer:** split off 10 coins and flip them all.

prompt: There are four prisoners in a dungeon. Tomorrow, they will be separated into a group of three in one room, and the other in a room by himself. Each will be given a hat to wear that is either black or white – two will be given white and two black. None of them will be able to communicate with each other and none will see his or her own hat color. The group of three is lined up, so that the one in the back can see the other two, the second can see the first, but the first cannot see the others. If anyone is certain of their hat color, then they immediately shout that they know it to the rest of the group. If they can secretly prove it to the guard, they are saved. They only say something if they're sure. Which person is sure to survive?

solutions.title: Reasoning from silence
solutions.body:
The person in back sees the other two in the room. If those two hats match (both white or both black), he knows his own hat is the other color, because there are only two of each, and he shouts.

If he stays silent, the two hats in front of him must differ.

The second person sees the first person's hat. If the back person shouts, the second person knows his hat matches the first person's. If the back person stays silent, he knows his hat is the opposite color. Either way he can be certain, so the second person is sure to survive.

**Answer: second in line**

prompt: Down the road, there are 10 prisoners in a dungeon. Tomorrow they will be lined up in a single room and each given a black or white hat – this time they don't know how many of each. The person in the back can see everyone's hat besides his own, and similarly everyone else can only see the hats of the people in front of them. The person in the back will shout out a guess for his hat color and will be saved if and only if he is right. Then the person in front of him will have to guess, and this will continue until everyone has the opportunity to be saved. Each person can only say his or her guess of “white” or “black” when their turn comes, and no other signals may be made. If they have the night before receiving the hats to try to devise some sort of code, how many people at a minimum can be saved with the most optimal code?

solutions.title: Parity code
solutions.body:
Code: the person in the back says “black” if he sees an odd number of white hats and “white” if he sees an even number. His own guess is right only by luck.

Each later person knows the parity of white hats among the 9 people in front of the back person. He sees the hats in front of him and has heard the (now correct) guesses of everyone behind him except the back person, so he can work out the parity of his own hat and says his color correctly.

So the 9 people in front are always saved. No code can guarantee the back person, who has no information about his own hat, so the minimum saved is 9.

**Answer: 9**
